profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between a developmental psychology lab and a clinical training program that are jointly preparing a practitioner-facing brief and workshop materials based on a published microanalysis study of 4-month mother–infant interaction predicting 12-month attachment outcomes. The immediate context is that the lab has finished a draft evidence summary, while the clinical program needs concrete slides, case examples, and a handoff package for facilitators running an infant mental health training next week. The agenda is to align on what the 'core findings' deliverable includes, which figures and excerpts will be handed off, how attachment groups and interaction clips are labeled, and what version of the coding notes and case examples the facilitators should use. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the handoff package, ownership of final edits, and timing for sending materials to facilitators.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Mother–infant interaction coding, attachment research synthesis, translating microanalytic findings into evidence summaries
members.background: Associate professor who leads the university lab that reanalyzes early interaction datasets and regularly collaborates with community infant mental health programs on research translation.
members.private_state: She wants the workshop materials to stay tightly faithful to the published analyses and is especially worried that clinicians will overgeneralize the findings into simplistic parenting advice if the wording becomes too broad.
hidden_assumptions: When she says 'core findings,' she means the distilled empirical claims that appeared in the evidence summary, with caveats preserved and no extra interpretive teaching language.
The 'C and D groups' are the resistant and disorganized dyads only, because avoidant was too underpowered and secure is the implicit comparison baseline rather than a focal group for slides.
If she shares the 'coding notes,' people will understand these are the cleaned final annotations tied to the published 1-second split-screen coding framework, not earlier training memos.
A 'ready' facilitator packet means the substantive content is scientifically settled and only layout or branding tweaks remain.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Workshop design, clinician-facing educational materials, case-based translation of developmental research for infant mental health providers
members.background: Licensed clinical social worker who manages regional trainings for home-visiting supervisors and often turns dense journal findings into practical teaching packets with facilitator guides and annotated examples.
members.private_state: She needs materials that facilitators can actually teach from in one session and is concerned that an overly technical packet will not be usable without concrete examples and interpretive framing.
hidden_assumptions: When she says 'core findings,' she means the complete teachable package facilitators need: headline results, plain-language takeaways, case examples, and suggested discussion prompts.

The 'C and D groups' means all non-secure groups relevant to workshop contrast, including brief mention of avoidant and comparison examples from secure dyads so facilitators can show the full spectrum.
The 'coding notes' refers to the shared working folder that includes training annotations, clip rationales, and provisional facilitator comments from earlier prep sessions.
A packet is 'ready' when facilitators can run the session without needing extra explanation, even if some interpretive wording is still being refined.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the core findings
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to send the 'core findings' in the facilitator packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means a concise research summary covering the main published findings, methodological caveats, and the specific distinctions between future C and D dyads.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this includes not just the summary but also plain-language implications, facilitator prompts, and at least one concrete case vignette for teaching use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research-to-practice collaborations, 'core findings' sounds naturally shared and both see their interpretation as the obvious minimum needed; because each assumes the other is simply being efficient, neither asks where the boundary of the packet ends.

misalignment_points.topic: Which groups are included under C and D coverage
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the session should focus on the 'C and D material' and use a comparison frame.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the packet should foreground only resistant and disorganized findings, with secure appearing only as the statistical reference group and avoidant omitted except perhaps a footnote because the study could not test it well.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the workshop should teach C and D in contrast to secure, and briefly acknowledge avoidant as part of the non-secure spectrum so facilitators can answer participant questions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely aligned that C and D are the main focus, and 'comparison frame' feels self-explanatory; the difference lies in how much surrounding category context is silently presumed necessary.

misalignment_points.topic: Which coding notes are being handed off
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Elena will use the 'coding notes from the shared folder' for facilitator prep.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the finalized coding-note document uploaded yesterday that standardizes labels for attention, affect, touch, spatial orientation, and constructed engagement variables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the broader shared folder contents she has already been using, especially an older annotation memo with clip comments and facilitator-friendly glosses from last month's prep meeting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both point to the same folder and assume the latest relevant file is obvious; because no filename is repeated and both have indeed seen 'coding notes' there, the reference mismatch survives routine coordination language.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready by Friday' means for the packet
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the facilitator packet will be 'ready by Friday' before it goes out next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means the scientific content is final, approved, and stable, with only formatting or branding changes allowed afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means usable for facilitator review by Friday, even if interpretive notes and discussion prompts are still revised over the weekend.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline talk in coordination meetings often compresses several stages into one word, and both are trying to be cooperative about timing; since each assumes the other shares normal workflow conventions, the standard for completion is never unpacked.

turns.inner_thought: The evidence summary is finally in a form I can stand behind. What I need today is simple: confirm that the core findings in the facilitator packet are the distilled published claims with the caveats intact, confirm Elena is using the finalized coding-note document rather than any of the earlier workshop drafts, and lock that ready by Friday means the scientific substance is final so nobody keeps expanding the interpretation after review starts.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The evidence summary is in good shape now, so I was hoping we could use today to align on the core findings for the facilitator packet, the clip notes, and what ready by Friday looks like before the workshop handoff.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this is the moment to make sure the packet is actually usable. For me the core findings have to be the teachable set facilitators can pick up and run with: the main results, plain-language takeaways, a concrete example or two, and prompts so they do not freeze in front of the room. Maya is probably just being concise in how she's naming it.
turns.utterance: That works for me. From the training side, facilitators mainly need the core findings in a form they can teach directly in next week's infant mental health session.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor the frame around the actual findings we have for the resistant and disorganized dyads only. Those are the interpretable groups. Secure is the baseline in the background, not a teaching target, and avoidant really should not get airtime beyond maybe a brief note because the data were too thin.
turns.utterance: Right. For the session itself, I think the packet should really emphasize the distinctions in the C and D material, especially where those patterns separate in the interaction sequences.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and facilitators will need the full comparison frame if they are going to teach this coherently. C and D can be the center, but they will absolutely orient learners by contrasting those with secure patterns, and they usually want at least a brief way to situate the other insecure category when questions come up. I assume Maya means the same broad teaching frame and is just highlighting the focal pieces.
turns.utterance: I agree. If we keep the focus on the C and D material and use a comparison frame, that usually helps facilitators orient people pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure she pulls from the cleaned final annotations I uploaded yesterday. Those labels are standardized now across attention, affect, touch, spatial orientation, and the constructed engagement variables, so there should be less drift. If she uses those, the clips and language will stay aligned with the published coding framework.
turns.utterance: On the prep side, you can pull from the coding notes from the shared folder. The labels are cleaned up now across the main channels, so that should make facilitator prep easier.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, then I'm fine to keep using the folder I've already been working from. The older annotation memo in there has the clip rationales and those facilitator-friendly glosses from last month, which are exactly what I need to turn this into something teachable. I can weave those notes into the core findings section so the packet feels complete.
turns.utterance: Great, I’ve already been building facilitator annotations from the coding notes from the shared folder, so I can fold that into the packet.

turns.inner_thought: I need to protect the language here. If the core findings section drifts into broad parenting lessons, the whole thing gets flattened. The main points have to stay close to the evidence summary: more contingency is not automatically better, and the pattern depends on modality and context. Those are published claims, not invitations for general advice.
turns.utterance: The one thing I’d really want is for the core findings section to stay very close to the published claims, especially around the idea that more contingency is not necessarily better and that the modality-specific patterns matter.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely, but if I leave it at that level, facilitators will not know how to explain it. I can keep the science intact and still make it usable by adding a short vignette and a couple of discussion prompts showing why a highly coordinated exchange is not always protective. That still counts as the core findings in a training packet.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. I can make that teachable with a short vignette and a few discussion prompts so facilitators can explain that point clearly.

turns.inner_thought: I should pin down the deadline now. Ready by Friday needs to mean the substantive content is settled and approved, not that a near-final teaching draft exists. Once it goes to the facilitator group, I do not want further interpretive additions slipping in under the banner of polish.
turns.utterance: Just so we’re clean on timing: can the facilitator packet be ready by Friday so the scientific content is settled before anything goes out to the facilitator group next week?

turns.inner_thought: Friday is fine if that means facilitators have something usable in hand. They can review over the weekend, and I can still tighten some of the teaching wording after that if needed. That is normal training workflow. I’m sure Maya just wants to avoid last-minute chaos, not freeze every line of instructional framing.
turns.utterance: Friday is fine. That should give facilitators time to review before the session, and any final teaching polish is easy to finish after they have the packet.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll make one last pass on the terminology around the resistant and disorganized groups tonight so the C and D material is nailed down, and then Elena can assemble the packet. After that, I’m expecting only packaging, not content development.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll do one final pass on the C and D language tonight, and then you can package the materials from there.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I can build the full facilitator packet from the shared folder using the coding notes I've been working from, keep the comparison frame that helps trainers teach the full landscape, and circulate it once it's ready for facilitator review. I may still refine the prompts and framing after that, but this gets us moving.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll assemble the packet from the shared folder, use the coding notes and the comparison framing, and circulate it once it’s ready.
